title: Action Potentials & Ion Channels
summary: How neurons turn ion gradients into fast electrical signals.

lessons.title: The Resting Membrane Potential

levels.kid:
Every neuron is like a tiny battery. When it is resting, the inside is a little bit negative compared with the outside.

Why? Tiny charged bits called **ions** are spread out unevenly. There is lots of **potassium** inside the cell and lots of **sodium** outside. A little machine called the **sodium-potassium pump** keeps it that way. It throws 3 sodium out and brings 2 potassium in, over and over, like a bouncer at a door.

Potassium can sneak out through little doors, and when it leaves it takes a bit of positive charge with it. That leaves the inside negative. This charged-up, ready state is what lets a neuron fire a message really fast.
levels.hs:
Neurons at rest have a voltage across their membrane called the **resting membrane potential**, typically about −70 millivolts (mV). The minus sign means the inside is negative relative to the outside.

Two things create it:

**1. Concentration gradients.** Ions are unevenly distributed. Potassium (K+) is high inside the cell; sodium (Na+), chloride (Cl−) and calcium (Ca2+) are high outside. The **Na+/K+ ATPase** (sodium-potassium pump) uses energy from ATP to pump 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in each cycle, maintaining these gradients.

**2. Selective permeability.** At rest, the membrane is much more permeable to K+ than to Na+ because of open "leak" K+ channels. K+ flows out down its concentration gradient. Each K+ that leaves carries a positive charge, making the inside more negative. Eventually the negative inside pulls back on K+ enough to balance the outward push. The voltage where those forces balance for an ion is its **equilibrium potential**. For K+ it is about −90 mV; for Na+ about +60 mV.

The resting potential (−70 mV) is close to K+'s equilibrium potential but slightly less negative, because a small amount of Na+ leaks in.

This matters clinically: if blood potassium rises (hyperkalemia), the K+ gradient shrinks and cells depolarize, which can cause dangerous heart rhythms.
levels.college:
**Equilibrium potentials.** For a single ion, the Nernst equation gives the voltage at which electrical and chemical driving forces balance: E = (RT/zF) ln([ion]out/[ion]in). At body temperature this simplifies to about 61.5/z × log10([out]/[in]) mV. With typical mammalian concentrations: E_K ≈ −90 mV, E_Na ≈ +60 mV, E_Cl ≈ −65 to −80 mV (cell-type dependent), E_Ca ≈ +120 mV or more.

**Multiple permeable ions.** The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz (GHK) equation weights each ion by its relative permeability. At rest, P_K : P_Na : P_Cl is roughly 1 : 0.04 : 0.45 (squid axon values often quoted), so V_rest sits near E_K but is pulled toward E_Na by Na+ leak. Changing a conductance moves the membrane toward that ion's equilibrium potential: opening K+ channels hyperpolarizes; opening Na+ channels depolarizes.

**Role of the pump.** The Na+/K+ ATPase is electrogenic (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in, net one positive charge out per cycle) and contributes directly only a few millivolts. Its main role is maintaining the gradients; block it (for example with ouabain or digoxin) and the potential slowly runs down.

**K+ leak channels.** Two-pore-domain K+ channels (K2P, e.g., TREK, TASK) and inward rectifiers (Kir) set the resting conductance. Volatile anesthetics activate some K2P channels, contributing to hyperpolarization.

**Driving force.** Current through a channel is I = g(Vm − E_ion). At −70 mV, Na+ has a large inward driving force (−70 − 60 = −130 mV), which is why opening Na+ channels produces a fast depolarization.

**Clinical.** Hyperkalemia shifts E_K less negative, depolarizing cells. Mild depolarization increases excitability, but sustained depolarization inactivates Na+ channels, reducing excitability, which is why severe hyperkalemia causes weakness and cardiac conduction failure.
levels.phd:
The resting potential is a steady state, not an equilibrium, and it is dynamically regulated.

**Steady state vs equilibrium.** No ion is at equilibrium at rest: Na+ continuously leaks in and K+ out, and the pump balances those fluxes at a metabolic cost. The GHK current equation assumes independent ion movement and a constant field; it fits many cells well but fails for channels with multi-ion pores and strong rectification. The chord-conductance form, Vm = Σ(g_i E_i)/Σg_i, is a useful approximation linking conductances to voltage.

**Chloride is cell-type specific.** E_Cl depends on cation–chloride cotransporters. Mature neurons express KCC2 (extruding Cl−), keeping intracellular Cl− low so GABA-A receptor opening hyperpolarizes or shunts. Immature neurons express more NKCC1, accumulating Cl− so GABA depolarizes. Downregulation of KCC2 after injury, in epilepsy and in neuropathic pain can make GABA less inhibitory or even excitatory, and NKCC1 inhibition with bumetanide has been explored, with mixed results, in neonatal seizures and autism.

**Energetics.** Restoring gradients consumes a large fraction of brain ATP; estimates attribute most signaling energy to postsynaptic currents and action potentials. Energy failure in ischemia stops the pump within minutes, leading to anoxic depolarization, massive glutamate release and Ca2+ overload.

**Spreading depolarization.** Near-complete depolarization of neurons and glia propagates slowly (millimeters per minute) through gray matter. It is thought to underlie migraine aura, and in injured brain (stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, trauma) clusters of spreading depolarizations expand infarcts.

**Extracellular K+ homeostasis.** During intense firing, extracellular K+ rises; astrocytes buffer it through Kir4.1 and the Na+/K+ ATPase. Impaired buffering (for example Kir4.1 mutations in EAST/SeSAME syndrome) promotes seizures. The membrane potential is therefore a property of a neuron–glia–vascular unit, not of a neuron alone.
levels.expert:
Clinicians meet the resting membrane potential mainly through electrolytes, toxins and ischemia.

**Potassium.** Hyperkalemia depolarizes resting membranes. In the heart this produces peaked T waves, then PR prolongation, QRS widening and ultimately a sine-wave pattern or asystole. The emergency principle: calcium salts stabilize the myocardial membrane (raising threshold) without lowering potassium; insulin with glucose and beta-2 agonists shift K+ into cells; binders, diuretics or dialysis remove it. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes and causes weakness, ileus and arrhythmias. Periodic paralysis syndromes (channelopathies of muscle Na+, Ca2+ or K+ channels) cause episodic weakness linked to potassium shifts.

**Sodium and the brain.** Plasma sodium changes act largely through osmotic water shifts rather than directly through resting potential. Acute hyponatremia causes cerebral edema with seizures and herniation risk; chronic hyponatremia corrected too fast causes osmotic demyelination syndrome. The neurological rule is that the speed of correction matters as much as the number.

**Ischemia.** Within seconds of complete flow loss, the EEG flattens; within minutes, pump failure leads to anoxic depolarization. The ischemic penumbra is tissue that is electrically silent but still has ion gradients, salvageable if flow returns. That is the physiological basis of "time is brain" and of perfusion imaging to select patients for thrombectomy.

**Spreading depolarizations** recorded with subdural electrode strips in patients with severe trauma or subarachnoid hemorrhage correlate with worse outcomes, an active research area in neurocritical care.

**Toxins and drugs.** Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase; toxicity causes nausea, visual changes and arrhythmias, and hyperkalemia in acute overdose. Volatile anesthetics hyperpolarize neurons partly through K2P channels.

**Pitfall:** a "normal" serum potassium can coexist with dangerous total-body potassium depletion in diabetic ketoacidosis, because acidosis shifts K+ out of cells. Insulin then drives it back in and can cause sudden hypokalemia.

keyPoints: Typical neuronal resting potential is about −70 mV (inside negative)
The Na+/K+ ATPase pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, maintaining gradients
At rest the membrane is most permeable to K+, so Vrest is near E_K (about −90 mV)
The Nernst equation gives one ion's equilibrium potential; the GHK equation combines several ions
Hyperkalemia depolarizes membranes and can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias

examples.tr: Moves the membrane toward E_K, hyperpolarizing it.
Stabilizes the cardiac membrane without lowering potassium.

lessons.title: Ion Channels

levels.kid:
Neurons have tiny doors in their skin called **ion channels**. Each door lets only one kind of ion through, like a door with a special key just for sodium or just for potassium.

Some doors open when the electricity changes. These are **voltage-gated** doors. Some doors open when a chemical messenger lands on them, like a key fitting a lock. These are **ligand-gated** doors. Some doors are always a little bit open. They are **leak** doors.

When the doors open, ions rush through and the neuron's charge changes. That is how a neuron gets ready to send a message. Some medicines and even some animal poisons work by jamming these doors shut!
levels.hs:
**Ion channels** are proteins that form pores through the cell membrane, allowing specific ions to pass. Without them, charged ions could not cross the fatty membrane. Channels have two key properties:

**1. Selectivity.** Each channel prefers certain ions. Sodium channels let Na+ through, potassium channels let K+ through, and so on. A narrow region called the **selectivity filter** decides which ions fit.

**2. Gating.** Channels open and close in response to signals:
- **Voltage-gated channels** open when the membrane voltage changes. Voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels create the action potential; voltage-gated Ca2+ channels trigger neurotransmitter release.
- **Ligand-gated channels** open when a chemical binds, such as the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction, which opens when acetylcholine binds.
- **Mechanically gated channels** open when stretched or pushed, as in touch receptors and the hair cells of the ear.
- **Leak channels** are mostly open and set the resting potential.

Ions move passively through channels, always down their electrochemical gradient. Pumps, in contrast, use energy to move ions against their gradients.

Many toxins target channels. **Tetrodotoxin**, found in pufferfish, blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels and can cause paralysis. Local anesthetics such as lidocaine also block Na+ channels, which is how a dentist numbs your mouth.
levels.college:
**Voltage-gated Na+ channels (Nav).** The α subunit is a single polypeptide of four homologous domains (DI–DIV), each with six transmembrane segments (S1–S6). S4 carries positively charged residues and acts as the voltage sensor; S5–S6 and the P-loop form the pore. A short intracellular loop between DIII and DIV (with the IFM motif) is the fast-inactivation gate. Nav channels therefore have three main states: closed (resting), open, and inactivated. Recovery from inactivation requires repolarization. Subtypes: Nav1.1/1.2/1.6 (CNS), Nav1.4 (skeletal muscle), Nav1.5 (heart), Nav1.7/1.8/1.9 (peripheral pain neurons).

**Voltage-gated K+ channels (Kv)** are tetramers of four separate α subunits, each with S1–S6. Delayed rectifiers repolarize the action potential; A-type currents (Kv4) shape firing frequency; Kv7 (M-current) stabilizes resting potential and is targeted by retigabine (ezogabine).

**Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Cav)** resemble Nav channels structurally. L-type (Cav1) channels mediate muscle contraction and are blocked by dihydropyridines; N-type (Cav2.2) and P/Q-type (Cav2.1) channels trigger neurotransmitter release at presynaptic terminals; T-type (Cav3) channels produce low-threshold bursts in thalamic neurons, relevant to absence seizures (ethosuximide blocks them).

**Ligand-gated channels.** Families include Cys-loop receptors (nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, glycine, 5-HT3: pentamers), ionotropic glutamate receptors (AMPA, NMDA, kainate: tetramers) and P2X ATP receptors (trimers).

**Other channels.** HCN channels carry the "funny current" (Ih), opened by hyperpolarization, producing pacemaker activity; TRP channels sense temperature and chemicals (TRPV1, capsaicin; TRPM8, menthol); Piezo channels sense mechanical force.

**Pharmacology.** Local anesthetics and several antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine) preferentially bind open or inactivated Na+ channels, giving use-dependent block that suppresses rapidly firing neurons more than normally firing ones.
levels.phd:
Structural biology has made ion channel gating a mechanistic science.

**Selectivity.** The K+ channel structure (KcsA, MacKinnon, 2003 Nobel Prize) showed a filter lined by backbone carbonyl oxygens (TVGYG signature) that mimic the hydration shell of K+ but are too far apart to coordinate the smaller Na+ ion efficiently, explaining a selectivity ratio of over 1000:1 together with fast conduction via multiple ions in single file. Nav channels use a DEKA ring (one residue from each domain) for Na+ selectivity; mutating it to EEEE converts the pore to Ca2+ selectivity.

**Voltage sensing.** S4 arginines move outward in steps through a hydrophobic constriction ("gating charge transfer center") as the membrane depolarizes, measured as gating currents. Cryo-EM structures of mammalian Nav and Cav channels in multiple states have clarified electromechanical coupling via the S4–S5 linker. In Nav channels, DIV S4 movement is especially coupled to fast inactivation.

**Channelopathies.** Gain and loss of function map to opposite diseases. SCN9A (Nav1.7) gain of function causes inherited erythromelalgia and paroxysmal extreme pain disorder; loss of function causes congenital insensitivity to pain, which motivated Nav1.7-selective analgesic programs (so far clinically disappointing, suggesting compensatory opioid signaling and target-engagement problems). SCN1A loss of function causes Dravet syndrome; SCN2A gain of function causes early infantile epilepsy whereas loss of function associates with autism. KCNQ2 loss causes neonatal epilepsy. CACNA1A causes episodic ataxia type 2, familial hemiplegic migraine type 1 and SCA6. Muscle channelopathies include SCN4A periodic paralysis and myotonia, and CLCN1 myotonia congenita.

**Modulation.** Auxiliary subunits (Navβ, Kvβ, Cavα2δ) tune trafficking and kinetics. Gabapentinoids bind α2δ-1, reducing Cav trafficking and presynaptic release rather than blocking the pore. Resurgent Na+ current, produced by an open-channel blocking particle, supports high-frequency firing in Purkinje cells.

**Toxins as tools.** Tetrodotoxin and saxitoxin occlude the outer Nav pore; scorpion α- and β-toxins trap voltage sensors; conotoxins block N-type Cav channels (ziconotide is a synthetic ω-conotoxin used intrathecally for pain).
levels.expert:
At the bedside, channel pharmacology explains how several neurological drugs work and why they fail.

**Sodium channel blockers.** Phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine and lacosamide (which enhances slow inactivation) treat focal epilepsy and, for carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, trigeminal neuralgia. They can aggravate absence and myoclonic seizures and, as above, Dravet syndrome. Combining two classic Na+ channel blockers adds side effects (dizziness, diplopia, ataxia) more than benefit. Carbamazepine carries a risk of severe cutaneous reactions linked to HLA-B*15:02, which is why genotyping is recommended before starting it in patients of at-risk ancestry.

**Calcium channel drugs.** Ethosuximide (T-type) is a first-line choice for childhood absence epilepsy. Gabapentin and pregabalin (α2δ ligands) are used for neuropathic pain. Nimodipine, an L-type blocker, is given after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage because it improves outcomes, even though it does not reliably prevent angiographic vasospasm.

**Local anesthetics.** Small, myelinated Aδ fibers and unmyelinated C fibers are blocked earlier than large motor fibers, so pain and temperature go before touch and motor function. Local anesthetic systemic toxicity begins with perioral numbness, tinnitus and agitation, then seizures and cardiovascular collapse; lipid emulsion is the rescue therapy.

**Toxins in the emergency department.** Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) and saxitoxin (paralytic shellfish poisoning) cause perioral paresthesia progressing to paralysis with intact consciousness; treatment is supportive, including ventilation. Ciguatoxin opens Na+ channels and causes the classic reversal of hot and cold sensation.

**Autoimmune channelopathies.** Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type Ca2+ channels, often with small cell lung cancer) causes proximal weakness that transiently improves with exertion and autonomic symptoms. Antibodies to the VGKC complex (LGI1, CASPR2) cause limbic encephalitis with faciobrachial dystonic seizures (LGI1) or neuromyotonia (CASPR2).

**Pitfall:** treating a patient with Lambert–Eaton like myasthenia without searching for a tumor misses the cancer.

keyPoints: Ion channels are selective pores; gating can be voltage, ligand or mechanical
Voltage-gated Na+ channels have closed, open and inactivated states
Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels at terminals (N, P/Q types) trigger transmitter release; T-type channels drive thalamic bursts
Na+ channel blockers include local anesthetics and several antiseizure drugs; tetrodotoxin blocks Na+ channels
Channelopathies (genetic or autoimmune) cause epilepsy, pain disorders, migraine, ataxia and muscle disease

examples.tr: Tetrodotoxin blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, causing paresthesias and paralysis.
Antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type Ca2+ channels reduce acetylcholine release.

lessons.title: The Action Potential

levels.kid:
An **action potential** is the message a neuron sends. It is a quick zap of electricity that zooms down the axon.

Here is how it works. First, the neuron gets poked by messages from its friends. If the poke is big enough to reach a line called the **threshold**, the neuron fires! If not, nothing happens. It is all or nothing, like a light switch, not a dimmer.

When it fires, sodium doors fly open and sodium rushes in. The inside turns positive. Then potassium doors open and potassium rushes out, and the inside turns negative again. For a tiny moment after, the neuron needs a rest before it can fire again.

All of this takes about one thousandth of a second. Super fast!
levels.hs:
An **action potential** is a brief, all-or-none electrical signal that travels along an axon. It lasts about 1–2 milliseconds and has clear phases:

1. **Resting state** (about −70 mV): voltage-gated channels are closed.
2. **Depolarization to threshold**: inputs nudge the membrane less negative. If it reaches **threshold** (often around −55 mV), the action potential fires. Below threshold, nothing propagates. This is the **all-or-none** rule: a stronger stimulus does not make a bigger action potential; it makes action potentials come more often.
3. **Rising phase**: voltage-gated Na+ channels open. Na+ rushes in, and the membrane shoots up to about +30 to +40 mV.
4. **Peak and falling phase (repolarization)**: Na+ channels inactivate (a gate closes), and voltage-gated K+ channels open. K+ flows out, bringing the voltage back down.
5. **Afterhyperpolarization (undershoot)**: K+ channels are slow to close, so the voltage dips below rest briefly before returning.

**Refractory periods:**
- **Absolute refractory period**: no new action potential can fire, because Na+ channels are inactivated.
- **Relative refractory period**: a new one can fire but needs a stronger-than-normal stimulus.

Refractory periods make action potentials travel in one direction and limit how fast a neuron can fire.

The mechanism was worked out in the 1950s by **Hodgkin and Huxley** using the giant axon of the squid, work that earned a Nobel Prize.
levels.college:
**Ionic basis.** Depolarization opens Nav channels; the inward Na+ current depolarizes further, opening more channels (positive feedback). Threshold is the voltage at which inward Na+ current exceeds outward K+ and leak current, so threshold is not fixed: it depends on channel availability and on how fast depolarization arrives (slow depolarization allows inactivation, raising threshold, called accommodation).

The peak approaches but does not reach E_Na because Na+ channels inactivate within about a millisecond and delayed-rectifier K+ channels open. Repolarization reflects Na+ inactivation plus K+ efflux. The afterhyperpolarization occurs because K+ conductance stays elevated, moving Vm toward E_K; Ca2+-activated K+ channels (BK, SK) contribute longer AHPs that regulate firing rate.

**Surprisingly few ions move.** A single action potential changes intracellular Na+ concentration negligibly in a large axon; the gradients persist for thousands of spikes even with pumps blocked. Ion movement is tiny relative to total ions; what changes is charge on the membrane capacitor.

**Hodgkin–Huxley model.** Using the voltage clamp, Hodgkin and Huxley separated Na+ and K+ currents and described them with voltage-dependent gating variables: m (Na+ activation, fast), h (Na+ inactivation, slower) and n (K+ activation). The Na+ conductance is proportional to m³h, the K+ conductance to n⁴. The model predicted the action potential's shape and conduction velocity from first principles.

**Refractoriness.** The absolute refractory period reflects Na+ channel inactivation; the relative refractory period reflects partial recovery of Na+ channels plus residual K+ conductance. This sets maximum firing frequencies of a few hundred hertz in most neurons.

**Coding.** Because amplitude is fixed, information is carried by firing rate, timing and patterns (bursts).

**Clinical.** Hypocalcemia lowers the threshold of nerve and muscle (extracellular Ca2+ screens surface charges on Na+ channels), causing tetany, perioral tingling, and Chvostek and Trousseau signs.
levels.phd:
The Hodgkin–Huxley framework still anchors the field, but the real action potential is more diverse and more interesting.

**Model limits.** HH gating assumes independent gates, while Nav activation and inactivation are coupled (inactivation is faster from partially activated states). Markov models with explicit states fit single-channel data better. Cortical action potentials have a sharper onset than HH predicts; explanations include initiation in the AIS with backpropagation into the soma ("lateral current") and cooperative Na+ channel gating; the first is better supported.

**Energy efficiency.** Squid axon spikes are energetically wasteful, with large overlap of Na+ and K+ currents. Mammalian neurons minimize this overlap by fast Na+ inactivation and delayed K+ activation, reducing ATP cost per spike several-fold, consistent with evolutionary pressure on brain energy budgets.

**Firing types.** Neurons differ in excitability class. Class I neurons can fire at arbitrarily low frequencies (saddle-node bifurcation); class II neurons begin firing at a non-zero frequency (Hopf bifurcation) and show resonance. Fast-spiking interneurons express Kv3 channels whose rapid deactivation allows very narrow spikes and firing rates of several hundred hertz. Thalamic relay neurons switch between tonic and burst modes via T-type Ca2+ channels and Ih, the cellular basis of sleep spindles and absence spike-wave discharges.

**Backpropagation and dendritic spikes.** Action potentials backpropagate into dendrites with attenuation set by dendritic K+ channels (A-type, Kv4.2), providing a timing signal for spike-timing-dependent plasticity.

**Analog modulation of digital signals.** Somatic subthreshold depolarization can spread down the axon and broaden presynaptic spikes, increasing transmitter release ("analog–digital" signalling) in hippocampal and cortical neurons, so the spike is not purely binary at the synapse.

**Ephaptic coupling.** Extracellular fields from synchronous activity can influence neighboring neurons without synapses, relevant in dense tissue and in demyelinated tracts where cross-talk can generate positive symptoms.
levels.expert:
Understanding the action potential lets clinicians read nerve tests, explain symptoms and predict drug effects.

**Nerve conduction studies** stimulate a nerve and record the summed action potentials of many axons: the compound muscle action potential (CMAP) for motor and the sensory nerve action potential (SNAP). Amplitude reflects the number of conducting axons; latency and velocity reflect myelin. A key localizing trick: in a radiculopathy (root lesion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion) the SNAP is preserved even though the patient is numb, because the sensory cell body and its peripheral axon are intact; in a plexopathy or peripheral nerve lesion the SNAP falls.

**Positive symptoms.** Demyelinated or irritable axons fire ectopically and can cross-talk, producing paresthesias, Lhermitte's sign in MS (an electric shock down the spine on neck flexion) and trigeminal neuralgia. Uhthoff's phenomenon, worsening of MS symptoms with heat, reflects temperature effects on channel kinetics: heat shortens action potentials and conduction fails in marginally functioning demyelinated axons.

**Electrolytes.** Hypocalcemia increases excitability: carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm and seizures; Trousseau's sign (carpal spasm with a blood-pressure cuff) is more specific than Chvostek's. Hypomagnesemia causes similar hyperexcitability and makes hypocalcemia and hypokalemia hard to correct until magnesium is replaced.

**In the operating room.** Motor evoked potentials and somatosensory evoked potentials rely on reliable action potential conduction. Volatile anesthetics and neuromuscular blockers suppress some of these signals, so neuromonitoring needs coordination with anesthesia; a sudden loss of signals during spine surgery prompts checking blood pressure, positioning and technical causes and, if real, reversing the last surgical maneuver.

**Toxicology.** Na+ channel blockade by tricyclic antidepressants widens the QRS complex and causes seizures and arrhythmias; sodium bicarbonate is the treatment because sodium loading and alkalinization overcome the block.

**Pitfall:** an EMG/NCS done in the first days after acute nerve injury can look normal distal to the lesion until Wallerian degeneration occurs.

keyPoints: Action potentials are all-or-none: threshold is reached or nothing propagates
Rising phase = Na+ influx through voltage-gated Na+ channels; falling phase = Na+ inactivation + K+ efflux
The undershoot (afterhyperpolarization) reflects persistent K+ conductance
Absolute refractory period: Na+ channels inactivated; relative: a stronger stimulus is needed
Stimulus intensity is coded by firing frequency, not action potential size

lessons.title: Conduction Velocity & Saltatory Conduction

levels.kid:
Some nerve messages travel slowly and some travel super fast. What makes the difference?

**Thicker wires are faster.** A wide axon is like a wide highway. Electricity flows through it more easily.

**Coated wires are faster.** Axons wrapped in myelin let the message jump from gap to gap, like a frog leaping across lily pads instead of swimming.

That is why, if you stub your toe, you feel the bump first and the throbbing ache a moment later. The "bump" message rides on fast, thick, coated wires. The "ouch" ache message rides on thin, uncoated wires that are much slower.

Doctors can even measure how fast your nerves send messages with a special test that uses tiny zaps.
levels.hs:
How fast an action potential travels, its **conduction velocity**, depends mainly on two things.

**1. Axon diameter.** Wider axons have less internal resistance, so current spreads farther ahead of the action potential, like water flowing through a wider pipe. This is why squids evolved giant axons for fast escape.

**2. Myelination.** Myelin insulates the axon, so the action potential only needs to regenerate at the **nodes of Ranvier**. The signal effectively leaps from node to node (**saltatory conduction**). Myelinated axons can be fast while staying thin, which saves space: a human spinal cord built only from unmyelinated axons would need to be enormously wider to get the same speeds.

**Nerve fiber types** (fastest to slowest):
- **Aα**: thick, heavily myelinated; muscle spindle sensors and motor neurons to muscle (about 80–120 m/s).
- **Aβ**: touch and vibration (about 35–75 m/s).
- **Aδ**: thinly myelinated; sharp, fast pain and cold (about 5–30 m/s).
- **C**: unmyelinated; dull, burning pain, warmth, itch and autonomic fibers (about 0.5–2 m/s).

This explains "first pain" (sharp, Aδ) followed by "second pain" (aching, C).

Temperature matters too: cooling slows conduction. Doctors measure conduction velocity with **nerve conduction studies**, where a nerve is stimulated at two points and the time difference is measured. Diseases that damage myelin, like Guillain–Barré syndrome, slow conduction dramatically.
levels.college:
**Cable properties.** Passive spread along an axon depends on membrane resistance (r_m), internal (axial) resistance (r_i) and membrane capacitance (c_m). The **length constant** λ = √(r_m/r_i) is the distance over which a passive voltage decays to about 37% (1/e); the **time constant** τ = r_m·c_m sets how quickly the membrane charges. Faster conduction comes from larger λ (current spreads farther) and smaller τ (membrane charges faster).

**Diameter.** Increasing diameter lowers r_i (proportional to 1/radius²) more than it lowers r_m, so λ grows. In unmyelinated axons velocity scales roughly with √diameter; in myelinated axons approximately linearly with diameter (a classic rule of thumb is about 6 m/s per µm of total fiber diameter in large mammalian fibers).

**Myelin.** Myelin greatly increases r_m and decreases c_m across internodes. Nav channels cluster at nodes (densities on the order of 1000/µm²) while internodes have very few. The action potential is regenerated at each node; internodal conduction is nearly instantaneous, so most delay occurs at nodes. Internodal length is around 100 times the fiber diameter, so a safety factor of several-fold ensures each node is depolarized well above threshold.

**Two classification systems.** Erlanger–Gasser (A, B, C; A subdivided α, β, γ, δ) applies to all fibers; B fibers are myelinated preganglionic autonomic axons. Lloyd–Hunt (I–IV) applies to sensory afferents from muscle: Ia (spindle primary) and Ib (Golgi tendon organ) correspond to Aα, II to Aβ, III to Aδ, IV to C.

**Demyelination effects.** Loss of myelin raises capacitance and lowers resistance at the internode, so current leaks before reaching the next node. Results range from slowed conduction to complete **conduction block**. Surviving demyelinated axons may redistribute Nav channels (including Nav1.2) along the bare membrane and restore continuous, slow conduction, part of recovery in MS.

**Temperature.** Cooling slows Nav gating, slowing conduction (about 1.5–2 m/s per °C in clinical studies), so limbs are warmed before nerve conduction testing to avoid false slowing.
levels.phd:
Conduction velocity is a tunable parameter used by the nervous system to time computation, not merely to be fast.

**Optimization.** Rushton's 1951 analysis predicted that myelination pays off only above a critical diameter of about 1 µm and that velocity is maximized at a g-ratio near 0.6. Peripheral axons fit this well, but CNS axons are myelinated down to about 0.2 µm. Many CNS axons are thinly myelinated relative to this optimum, implying trade-offs with space and energy. Internode length also has an optimum: velocity is relatively flat around the natural length, which makes conduction robust to variation.

**Timing precision.** In the auditory brainstem, axons to the medial superior olive are tuned in diameter and internode length so inputs from both ears arrive within microseconds, enabling interaural time difference coding. In the cerebellum and thalamocortical projections, conduction delays are equalized across axons of different lengths, producing synchronous arrival. Activity-dependent myelination could adjust these delays during learning; modeling suggests this would tune oscillatory synchrony between regions.

**Node and internode microstructure.** Node length and periaxonal space width vary across axons and modulate velocity by tens of percent in simulations, providing additional tuning knobs beyond myelin thickness. Nodal Nav1.6 versus Nav1.2 composition affects resurgent current and high-frequency following.

**Pathophysiology of demyelination.** Conduction block depends on the safety factor. Demyelinated segments show frequency-dependent conduction failure (they can conduct single spikes but fail during trains), explaining fatigability. Redistributed Nav1.6 channels along demyelinated axons can produce a persistent Na+ current that drives reverse Na+/Ca2+ exchange and Ca2+ loading, a proposed mechanism of axonal degeneration in progressive MS. Ectopic generators and ephaptic transmission along demyelinated segments produce paroxysmal symptoms.

**Unmyelinated fibers.** C-fiber velocity is activity-dependent: repetitive firing progressively slows conduction (activity-dependent slowing, related to Nav1.7/1.8 slow inactivation and Na+/K+ pump hyperpolarization), and the pattern differs between mechano-insensitive "silent" nociceptors and other C-fiber classes, which microneurography can distinguish in humans.
levels.expert:
Nerve conduction studies are the clinical readout of conduction velocity, and the patterns localize disease.

**Axonal vs demyelinating.**
- **Axonal** neuropathy: reduced CMAP and SNAP amplitudes with velocities normal or only mildly reduced (losing the fastest fibers drops velocity modestly). EMG shows denervation and later reinnervation. Typical causes: diabetes, alcohol, toxins, chemotherapy, critical illness.
- **Demyelinating** neuropathy: marked slowing (commonly below about 70–75% of the lower limit of normal), prolonged distal motor latencies, prolonged or absent F-waves, conduction block and temporal dispersion.

**Uniform vs patchy demyelination.** Hereditary demyelinating neuropathy (CMT1A) slows all nerves uniformly, without conduction block, because every Schwann cell carries the defect. Acquired demyelination (Guillain–Barré, CIDP) is patchy, with conduction block and dispersion. This distinction helps separate inherited from treatable immune-mediated disease.

**Early Guillain–Barré.** The earliest finding is often prolonged or absent F-waves (reflecting proximal root involvement) with a normal-looking distal study. Studies can be normal in the first days; diagnosis is clinical, supported by CSF protein elevation without many cells. Axonal variants (acute motor axonal neuropathy, linked to Campylobacter jejuni and anti-GM1 antibodies) show low amplitudes.

**Entrapments.** Carpal tunnel syndrome shows focal slowing across the wrist: prolonged median distal latencies, sensory first. Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow shows focal slowing across the elbow segment. Focal slowing localizes the site of compression for surgery.

**Technical pitfalls.** Cold limbs falsely slow conduction and raise amplitudes; warm the limb. Wrong electrode placement, anomalous innervation (Martin–Gruber anastomosis) and older age all change values. Sural SNAPs can be absent in healthy older adults.

**Small-fiber disease is invisible** to NCS, which records large myelinated fibers; skin biopsy or autonomic testing is needed.

**For neurosurgery:** intraoperative nerve action potentials across a lesion in continuity show whether regenerating axons cross it, guiding whether to resect and graft.

keyPoints: Conduction velocity rises with axon diameter and with myelination
Saltatory conduction: the action potential regenerates only at nodes of Ranvier
Fiber types fastest to slowest: Aα, Aβ, Aδ, C (unmyelinated)
First (sharp) pain travels on Aδ fibers; second (burning) pain on C fibers
Nerve conduction studies distinguish axonal (low amplitude) from demyelinating (slow velocity, block) neuropathy
